newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Pol Pot expected to live quietly under house arrest.
newsitem.headline: Pol Pot expected to live quietly under house arrest.

text.p: Hated Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot is likely to live out his life quietly with his family despite being condemned and apparently sentenced to life in detention for his crimes, analysts said on Wednesday.
Pol Pot, now almost 70, was denounced by his former comrades at a "show trial" and mass rally in a north Cambodian jungle clearing on Friday and sentenced to house arrest for life.
But the punishment should not be much of a burden for a sick old man responsible for the death of more than one million people during the Khmer Rouge's "killing fields" rule from 1975-79.
Pol Pot is being held in the guerrillas' Anlong Veng base in remote territory near the border with Thailand.
"Basically, he's been politically purged but in practice it may not mean that much," said Cambodia scholar David Ashley.
"They don't really have a place of long-term detention," he said of the Khmer Rouge guerrillas who turned against Pol Pot after a bloody split among the group's top leaders in June.
"My guess is that they'll keep him in his old house and will probably allow his family to stay with him," he said. "But previously he was fairly immobile anyway, he didn't travel much."

Pol Pot married for a second time in the early 1980s after his first wife suffered a breakdown. His second wife, a former squad leader of women ammunition porters, is believed to be more than 20 years younger than him. They have two children.
At his Friday trial, Pol Pot was condemned for a catalogue of crimes, including the June massacre of Khmer Rouge defence chief Son Sen and 11 members of his family.
American journalist Nate Thayer reported witnessing the scene and said that although it was stage-managed, Pol Pot's denunciation was genuine and the radical Khmer Rouge of old were finished.
Thayer said Pol Pot looked frail and distraught and had to be helped away by guards after his sentence was handed down.
The veteran communist, who has lived in Cambodia's jungles for decades, is said to suffer from malaria and other ailments.
In Phnom Penh, powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen dismissed Pol Pot's trial as a political game and said he was still the secretive group's real leader.
Analysts said if Pol Pot had been condemned, then the new leader of the guerrilla group was someone equally ruthless, chief military commander Ta Mok.

"If Pol Pot has been toppled then they'll keep him in a safe house, somewhere along the border with Thailand, near Anlong Veng, and that will be it," said long-time Khmer Rouge watcher Christphe Peschoux.
"Most of the leadership have lived like that for years anyway," he said.
"But we're missing the point if we focus on this trial and Pol Pot's removal," Peschoux said. "The main point is who is in charge now, and if Pol Pot is not in charge, that means Ta Mok is."
"Ta Mok is less sophisticated than Pol Pot, as ruthless and as, if not more, radical than Pol Pot," he said.
The one-legged Ta Mok became knows as "the butcher of Cambodia" for his cold efficiency in carrying out Pol Pot's purges.

After Pol Pot and his government were forced from power by a Vietnamese army of invasion in early 1979, Ta Mok ended up in Cambodia's remote north, protected by the area's huge forests and profiting from the sale of trees to Thailand.
After a major split in the Khmer Rouge in August last year the hardcore remnants of the group were forced to seek refuge at Ta Mok's Anlong Veng headquarters where he still reins supreme.
"Both of them have so much blood on their hands," Ashley said of Pol Pot and Ta Mok.
"Pol Pot was always the strategist and for the most part Ta Mok followed him."
